title: Enums vs literal unions with as const; type aliases vs interfaces
summary: Enums are the one everyday TypeScript feature that generates code, with quirks to match; a literal union derived from an `as const` array or object gives the same safety and is plain erasable JavaScript. Use interfaces for object shapes and type aliases for unions.

examples.title: What an enum is at run time, and where it leaks

annotations.note: A numeric enum compiles to an object holding both Debug -> 0 and 0 -> "Debug". Code that iterates Object.keys or Object.values over it sees six entries for three members, a classic source of duplicated dropdown options.

Since TS 5.0 an out-of-range literal is an error, but a value of type number is still assignable to a numeric enum. A 7 from the database type-checks as a Level, and the reverse lookup gives undefined.

String enums are an exception to structural typing: the literal "active" is not assignable to Status even though Status.Active is exactly "active" at run time. Every value from JSON needs a cast, and the cast checks nothing.

examples.title: The erasable replacement: as const and a derived union

annotations.note: as const (TS 3.4) makes the array a readonly tuple of literal types, and (typeof LEVELS)[number] reads the union of its elements back out. One source of truth: add a level to the array and the type follows.

includes on a tuple of literals only accepts those literals, so checking an arbitrary string needs a widened view. The `s is Level` return type is a type guard (lesson ts.narrowing.guards): a true result narrows s.

The other side of the Turkish rule: "INFO".toLocaleLowerCase("tr") is "ınfo" with a dotless ı, which matches nothing. Use the locale for words people read and plain toLowerCase() for ASCII identifiers.

The object form gives named members (Status.Active) like an enum, but the type is the plain union "active" | "suspended". A value and a type may share the name Status because they live in separate namespaces.

Interfaces describe object shapes and extend each other; a union of them needs a type alias, because an interface can only name an object type. This interface-per-variant plus union is the discriminated union you will use constantly.

Two interface declarations with the same name merge. That is how libraries let you add fields to Window or to a request type, and also how a stray duplicate name silently changes a type. Type aliases can't be reopened: declaring one twice is a "Duplicate identifier" error.

extends checks the new members against the base and reports the conflict where it is written. An intersection reports nothing: the member becomes never, and the error appears later, at whichever value fails to fit.

use_cases: Closed sets of values that cross the wire (statuses, roles, log levels): a const array or object plus its derived union
Runtime lists of the allowed values (validation, dropdowns) from the same as const array as the type
interface for object shapes, especially ones others may extend or augment; type for unions, tuples, functions and computed types
strengths: Literal unions cost nothing at run time and accept plain strings from JSON without casts, unlike string enums
as const keeps the runtime list and the type in one place, which Go needs a named type, iota constants and a hand-written slice for
Unlike Java's enum classes, a union of string literals is just data: it serialises to itself and needs no valueOf/name mapping
weaknesses: Unions have no namespace of named members unless you add the as const object; refactoring a string value means finding its uses by type, not by symbol
Enums give named members and IDE navigation, but emit code, break Node's type stripping and erasableSyntaxOnly, and numeric ones accept any number
type vs interface overlaps heavily, so codebases need a convention; declaration merging can surprise when two files reuse a name

pitfalls.title: Iterating a numeric enum
pitfalls.detail: Object.keys/values on a numeric enum include the reverse-mapping keys. Iterate an as const array instead.

pitfalls.title: Casting JSON strings to string enums
pitfalls.detail: `value as Status` compiles for any string and validates nothing. With a literal union, validate once with a guard like isLevel.

pitfalls.title: Locale-aware lowercasing of identifiers
pitfalls.detail: toLocaleLowerCase() with a Turkish default locale turns "INFO" into "ınfo". Lowercase ASCII identifiers with toLowerCase(); keep the "tr" locale for human text.

pitfalls.title: Intersections instead of extends for overriding a member
pitfalls.detail: `A & { id: number }` with A.id: string yields never instead of an error. Use interface extends (or Omit<A, "id"> & ...) when a member's type changes.

quiz.q: With erasableSyntaxOnly on, which declaration is an error?
quiz.why: enum (including const enum) generates JavaScript, so tsc reports TS1294. The others are erasable.

quiz.q: `enum Status { Active = "active" }`. Does `const s: Status = "active"` compile?
quiz.why: String enum types are nominal: only Status.Active is assignable, not the equal string literal.

quiz.q: `const LEVELS = ["debug", "info"] as const`. What is `(typeof LEVELS)[number]`?
quiz.why: as const keeps the literal types; indexing the tuple type with number gives the union of its elements.

quiz.q: When must you use a type alias rather than an interface?
quiz.why: An interface can only declare an object type; unions, tuples and primitive aliases need type.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: Everyday Types (type aliases vs interfaces, literal types)

body:
## Concept

TypeScript offers two ways to model a closed set of values:

- **`enum`**: named members compiled to a JavaScript object. Numeric enums also get a
  reverse mapping; string enums are nominal (only `Status.Active` is a `Status`).
- **A literal union**: `type Level = "debug" | "info" | "warn"`. To get a runtime list or
  named members as well, declare an array or object `as const` and derive the union
  from it with `(typeof X)[number]` or `(typeof X)[keyof typeof X]`.

`enum` is one of the few TypeScript constructs that is not erasable, which is why
`erasableSyntaxOnly` (TS 5.8) rejects it, `const enum` included, and why Node's type
stripping refuses to run it. The `as const` pattern gives the same compile-time safety
in plain JavaScript.

The second half of the lesson is the everyday choice between **`interface`** and
**`type`**. Both name object shapes. Only `type` can name a union, tuple, function or
computed type; only `interface` can be extended with `extends` checks and reopened by
declaration merging.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: enums there are classes with behaviour. TS string enums are closer to a set of
  constants with nominal typing; literal unions are closer to a sealed set of string
  values with no class at all.
- C/C++: numeric enums behave like C's `enum`: any integer value converts in, so the
  enum type does not guarantee a valid member. Even C++'s `enum class` is stricter; it
  needs a `static_cast`.
- Go: there are no enums. `type Level string` plus constants (or `iota`) is the idiom,
  and like a numeric TS enum it accepts any value of the underlying type through a
  conversion. `as const` plus a union is the TS idiom that plays the same role.
- Python: `Literal["debug", "info"]` is the literal union; `enum.Enum` is closer to TS
  enums, minus the reverse-mapping quirk.
- SQL: Postgres has `CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM` and CHECK constraints; a literal union is
  the TS-side mirror of a `CHECK (status IN ('active', 'suspended'))`.

## Design notes

Default to literal unions. Declare the values once `as const`, derive the type, and
validate untrusted strings with a guard built on the same array. That keeps the code
erasable (Node, esbuild and every other per-file tool run it unchanged), JSON values
flow in without casts, and the list of allowed values is available at run time for
validation and UI. Reach for an `enum` only when a codebase already uses them
consistently.

For object shapes, pick one convention and keep it. The handbook's heuristic is "use
`interface` until you need features from `type`": interfaces keep their names in error
messages and `extends` is checked, while unions, tuples, functions and mapped types
need `type`. The difference matters in two places: an interface
can be merged and augmented, which libraries rely on, and `extends` reports a conflicting
member where an intersection silently produces `never`.
